animal-liberation: The view, most famously argued by Peter Singer, that the suffering of animals counts morally on a par with similar human suffering. On this view, species membership alone — mere 'speciesism' — is no better a reason to disregard an animal's pain than race would be to disregard a human's, which many take to condemn factory farming and much animal experimentation.
aquinas-double-effect: A principle from Thomas Aquinas about actions that produce both good and harmful effects. It holds that such an act can be permissible if the harm is merely foreseen rather than intended, the act itself is not wrong, and the intended good is proportionate to the harm. It is widely invoked in debates about self-defense and risky rescue.
aristotle-four-causes: Aristotle's answer to what a full explanation of anything involves. To understand a thing, he held, you should know four things: what it is made of (material cause), what shape or structure it has (formal cause), what brought it about (efficient cause), and what it is for — its purpose or function (final cause). Purpose was, for him, built into nature itself.
benjamin-aura: The philosopher Walter Benjamin argued that an artwork traditionally had an 'aura': the unique presence of an original, tied to its history and to ritual or tradition. Photography and film, which make endless copies, strip this aura away while making art available to the many. Whether that is a loss or a liberation was, for Benjamin, an open question.
black-skin-white-masks: Frantz Fanon's 1952 study of what racism does to the mind. Fanon, a Martinican psychiatrist, described how a colonial world fixes Black people beneath a white gaze, forcing them to wear 'masks' of the colonizer's language and expectations, and how this dehumanization is built into social perception itself — not just into laws or individual prejudice.
confucian-li: In Confucian thought, li is ritual propriety: the inherited patterns of respectful conduct — manners, ceremonies, family duties — that give social life its shape. On the Confucian view these forms are not empty etiquette; practicing them trains feeling and habit, so that doing the outwardly proper thing helps a person become genuinely humane.
dewey-democracy: The American philosopher John Dewey held that democracy is not primarily a form of government but a way of life: a habit of cooperative inquiry, open communication, and shared problem-solving that runs through families, schools, and workplaces, not just elections. On this view democracy rests on faith in the intelligence and growth of ordinary people.
food-ethics: The branch of ethics that asks how we ought to eat: whether the pleasure of a food can justify the suffering or death it requires, what factory farming and environmental costs demand of us, and who is responsible — consumers, corporations, or states. It draws on utilitarian, Kantian, and virtue-based arguments alike, and its central questions remain unsettled.
hegel-recognition: G.W.F. Hegel argued that selves are not self-made islands: we become fully aware of ourselves only through another person's recognition of us as free and equal. His master-slave dialectic dramatizes this — a master who wins only slavish, coerced acknowledgment never gets the recognition he needs — an idea later thinkers extended into theories of identity, justice, and social struggle.
heraclitean-flux: The ancient Greek Heraclitus taught that everything flows (panta rhei): the world is ceaseless change, so that you cannot step into the same river twice. Yet he also spoke of the logos — a hidden rational order governing the flux, in which strife and opposition are somehow just. Stability, on this picture, is a surface appearance over deeper becoming.
kant-respect: For Immanuel Kant, persons have dignity rather than price: each rational being is an end in himself or herself, never to be treated merely as a means. Respect for persons therefore rules out deception, coercion, and manipulation, whatever the payoff — and it applies to how we treat ourselves, since self-respect is also a duty.
kingdom-of-ends: Kant's image of the moral world at its best: a 'kingdom of ends' in which all rational beings legislate the same universal laws for themselves and treat one another always as ends, never merely as means. Few think it can be fully realized; it functions as a regulative ideal against which our laws, institutions, and choices are measured.
memetics: Richard Dawkins coined the 'meme' in 1976 as a unit of culture — a tune, catchphrase, belief, or practice — spread by imitation, mutating and competing for minds much as genes compete under natural selection. Memetics treats cultural change as an evolutionary process; critics question whether 'memes' are real, well-defined units, so the idea remains controversial.
mill-liberty: John Stuart Mill's On Liberty (1859) defends near-complete freedom of thought and lifestyle. His harm principle says society may coerce an individual only to prevent harm to others — never for that person's own good or because the majority disapproves. Mill also argued that silencing an opinion assumes infallibility, and that truth sharpens itself against error.
paradigm-shift: Historian and philosopher of science Thomas Kuhn argued that science does not simply accumulate facts. Long stretches of 'normal science' work within a shared framework — a paradigm — until accumulating anomalies force a revolutionary shift to a new one, as when Copernicus displaced Ptolemy. Rival paradigms, he controversially held, are partly incommensurable: each shapes what its adherents can see and say.
parfit-teleportation: Derek Parfit's thought experiment: you step into a teleporter that scans and destroys your body while building an exact replica on Mars. Did you travel, or did you die and a copy wake up? Parfit used such cases to argue that personal identity is psychological continuity, comes in degrees, and may matter less than we assume. No consensus exists.
pragmatic-method: The method of the American pragmatists Peirce and James: to make a concept clear, ask what practical difference it would make — what to expect and how to act if it were true. On this method, a distinction with no conceivable practical consequences is no real distinction, and ideas earn their keep through their consequences.
racial-contract: Charles Mills's 1997 rewrite of classic social contract theory. He argued the historical contract was in practice among white people: an agreement, largely tacit, to constitute society as a white-supremacist order and to maintain it through an 'epistemology of ignorance' — a learned blindness to the realities of racial domination. The contract, on this view, predates and misshapes any genuine political agreement.
rousseau-natural-goodness: Rousseau broke with Hobbes by holding that humans are naturally good: endowed with self-preservation and spontaneous compassion, not innate aggression. It is society — above all property, inequality, and the restless comparing of ourselves with others — that corrupts us. His famous claim, 'man is naturally good, and only by institutions is he made bad,' anchors this tradition.
rousseau-social-contract: In The Social Contract (1762) Rousseau asked how people can live under laws yet remain free. His answer: legitimate authority rests on the general will — the collective will of the people aimed at the common good — to which each citizen submits equally. Hence 'man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains': most existing states fail this test.
sartre-freedom: Jean-Paul Sartre held that we are 'condemned to be free': with no God-given essence or script, we create ourselves through our choices, and we bear total responsibility for them — even for how we respond to what we did not choose. Escaping into excuses, roles, or 'that's just how I am' is what Sartre called bad faith.
ship-of-theseus: An ancient puzzle from Plutarch: the ship of the hero Theseus has every plank replaced over the years until no original material remains. Is it still the same ship? And if the old planks are reassembled into a vessel, which one — if either — is the original? The puzzle probes what personal and material identity through change could even consist in.
state-of-nature: A thought experiment central to social contract theory: what would human life be like without any government? Hobbes imagined a war of all against all; Locke a mostly peaceful condition where property is still insecure; Rousseau an independent, self-sufficient existence. The answers were never meant as history — they are devices for explaining what political authority is for.
watchmaker-argument: William Paley's 1802 argument for God: cross a heath and find a stone, and you shrug; find a watch, with its intricate, purpose-fit parts, and you infer a watchmaker. Since living organisms are vastly more intricate, Paley concluded that nature, too, has an intelligent designer. Hume's skepticism and Darwin's theory of natural selection are the standard challenges to it.
